nameStory: Morton's cockle gets its name from the naturalist Samuel George Morton, a 19th-century scientist who studied mollusks along the Atlantic coast. The "egg cockle" part comes from its smooth, oval shell that resembles a small bird's egg when closed. This sets it apart from other cockles that have prominent ribs or ridges decorating their shells.
description: Morton's cockle is a small, heart-shaped clam that lives buried in sandy ocean bottoms along New England's coast. When both shell halves are closed together, it looks remarkably like a smooth, cream-colored egg about the size of a large marble. Like all cockles, it's a filter feeder that pumps water through its body to catch tiny floating food particles. You're most likely to find empty shells washed up on beaches after storms.

idTips.label: Smooth shell surface
idTips.description: The shell feels completely smooth to your fingertips, lacking the prominent ribs or ridges found on most other cockles - it's as slick as a polished stone

idTips.label: Egg-like shape
idTips.description: When closed, the shell forms a perfect oval that looks exactly like a small bird's egg, fitting comfortably in your palm

idTips.label: Heart-shaped profile
idTips.description: Viewed from the side with the hinge at top, the shell forms a classic heart shape that gives all cockles their family nickname

idTips.label: Cream to tan coloring
idTips.description: Fresh shells range from creamy white to light tan or yellowish-brown, often with a subtle glossy sheen when wet

idTips.label: Size and weight
idTips.description: Typically marble-sized, feeling surprisingly light and delicate in your hand compared to the heavier, chunkier shells of other cockles

habitat: Morton's cockles live in shallow sandy or muddy bottoms in protected bays, estuaries, and nearshore waters from the low tide zone down to about 30 feet deep. They prefer areas with gentle currents where they can filter-feed effectively while staying buried. You'll find their empty shells washed up on sandy beaches throughout coastal New England, especially after storms stir up the seafloor.

seasonality.spring: Storm-tossed shells from winter begin appearing on beaches as the weather calms. Living cockles become more active in warming waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for finding fresh, intact shells on beaches during calm weather. Living cockles are most active in the warm water.
seasonality.fall: Autumn storms frequently wash shells ashore, making this an excellent season for beach collecting as rough seas disturb the sandy bottom.
seasonality.winter: Harsh winter storms regularly deposit shells on beaches, though the cockles themselves retreat deeper into the sand in colder water.

funFact: Morton's cockles can actually jump! When threatened, they use their powerful muscular foot to suddenly push against the sand and leap several inches through the water - imagine a clam doing gymnastics to escape a hungry crab.
confusionNotes: The smooth shell easily distinguishes Morton's cockle from other cockles, which have prominent ribs like a folding fan. However, it can be confused with small quahogs or other smooth clams - remember that cockles are heart-shaped when viewed from the side, while quahogs are more circular.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "egg cockles," these aren't actually related to bird eggs at all - the name purely describes their appearance. The cockle family gets its name from the heart shape, as "cockle" comes from an old word meaning "heart," as in the phrase "warm the cockles of your heart."
compareHints: Morton's cockle is the only egg cockle species found in New England waters, making it unique in its genus here. Compared to other cockles in the true cockle family, it's much smoother - while Atlantic strawberry cockles and prickly cockles have obvious ribs and bumps, Morton's cockle looks like nature polished it smooth. Think of it as the "minimalist" member of a very decorative family.
